required_claims.claim: rationale=Both worked demonstrations are forex pairs on the 15-minute chart, and the educator explicitly frames the forex market as what he has been showing while asserting broad applicability across assets.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now as I said at the beginning of the video this strategy is applicable to basically all assets. So of course the forex market like I've been showing you here today.

required_claims.claim: direction=both
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, anything above 50% of the trading range is considered premium and we should only be looking for selling opportunities. Now, anything below the 50% is considered discount pricing and we would only want to be looking for buying opportunities.

required_claims.claim: higher_timeframe=4 hour
required_claims.transcript_quote: And the 4our time frame is going to act as our higher time frame to form a bias and anchor that bias to at all times.

required_claims.claim: execution_timeframe=15-minute
required_claims.transcript_quote: The 15-minut time frame is going to be our execution time frame where we actually place trades.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (non-executable framing): the educator introduces this as a 15-minute strategy he claims is applicable to almost every asset and which he says produces opportunities weekly.
required_claims.transcript_quote: This strategy is applicable to almost every asset in the market, and it creates trading opportunities every single week.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the first worked example is demonstrated on GBP AUD on the 15-minute time frame.
required_claims.transcript_quote: We're taking a look at GBP AUD on the 15-minute time frame.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the second worked example is demonstrated on NZDUSD on the 15-minute time frame.
required_claims.transcript_quote: All right, we're now taking a look at NZDUSD on the 15-minute time frame.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the strategy is stated to use two time frames, the 15-minute and the 4 hour.
required_claims.transcript_quote: This strategy consists of two time frames, the 15-minute and the 4 hour.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the two time frames are required to work together in congruence.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Those need to work together in congruence.

required_claims.claim: description=Context/rationale (non-executable): the educator's stated reason for aligning the 15-minute bias to the higher time frame bias.
required_claims.transcript_quote: If we can align our 15minute trade bias to a higher time frame bias, which is the overarching trend, then more times than not, we'll be on the right side of the market, and it'll prevent a lot of unnecessary losses.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the taught checklist consists of four line items.
required_claims.transcript_quote: We have higher time frame alignment, liquidity sweep, break of structure plus imbalance, and a 71% retracement.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the educator states the underlying premise of the strategy.
required_claims.transcript_quote: The strategy is very simplistic. We buy low and sell high.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling note: the annotations shown on the chart come from a custom indicator the educator had coded, which automates the charting work.
required_claims.transcript_quote: This is a custom indicator that I've had coded and it basically just automates the charting process by creating these annotations for me so I don't have to do any manual chart work.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling note: the indicator is stated to be optional and everything taught can be done manually.
required_claims.transcript_quote: It's a great tool to have, but you don't need it. You can do all of the things I'm about to teach you today manually on your own.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling note: a free substitute for the indicator's structure arrows is named.
required_claims.transcript_quote: There's a free version of these little arrows if you search on Trading View fractals or Williams fractals.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example, tooling reading): in the GBP AUD example the educator's indicator checks premium and discount on the higher time frame, with that setting on 4hour.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, my indicator automatically checks premium and discount on the higher time frame. As you can see here, I have it set to 4hour.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example, tooling reading): in the NZDUSD example the indicator shows the 4hour time frame at a discount, which the educator ties to not looking for selling opportunities.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Well, my indicator is showing me that the 4hour time frame is currently at a discount, which means we should not be looking for selling opportunities.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): liquidity is described as resting money in the market.
required_claims.transcript_quote: The simple way to describe liquidity is just resting money in the market.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): liquidity purged to the upside is referred to as buyside liquidity.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So this is what's referred to as buyside liquidity because the liquidity was purged to the upside.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example reasoning): after the upside purge the educator states price's next objective would be to purge liquidity from the downside.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So now the next objective of price would be to purge liquidity from the downside.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling note: the indicator prints a BOS label when a structural low or high is violated.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So whenever one of these structural lows or highs vice versa is violated, you'll see this BOS label printed, which of course stands for break of structure.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): an imbalance / fair value gap is described as a three candlestick pattern with a gap between the low of the first candle and the high of the third candle.
required_claims.transcript_quote: it's a three candlestick pattern. 1 2 3. And between the low of this first candle and the high of the third candle, we can see that there is a very large gap.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): once an imbalance forms, price is described as being drawn back towards it.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now, whenever this occurs on the chart, price is drawn back towards it.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): after moving away, price is described as typically retracing to fill the gap and then often continuing in its intended direction.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, after we move away from it significantly, typically price will retrace until it fills that gap and then it will often continue in its intended direction.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (non-executable framing): the educator states the Fibonacci retracement tool is used only as a measurement tool, not as an indicator or a strategy.
required_claims.transcript_quote: The Fibonacci retracement tool is not an indicator. It is not a strategy in and of itself. The way I use it is simply as a measurement tool.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (non-executable framing): the educator explicitly denies that the retracement levels are reaction-producing magic numbers.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So don't be under the impression that somehow these retracement levels are magic numbers that price will react to. That is absolutely not the case.

required_claims.claim: description=Context: the educator names 71% as his favorite retracement number.
required_claims.transcript_quote: My favorite number to use is 71%.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (educator's stated risk-to-reward claim for the 71% framing).
required_claims.transcript_quote: If I target the 71% from my entry, I get a risk-to-reward ratio of 2.45.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling note: the TradingView magnet tool is recommended, set to weak magnet rather than strong magnet.
required_claims.transcript_quote: To make this easier, you can use the magnet tool on Trading View. Just set it to weak magnet instead of strong magnet.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable platform logistics: the entry, take-profit and stop-loss prices are read off the position-tool parameters and copied to the execution platform.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Then all you have to do is double click on the parameters and copy these prices over the entry price, the takerit, the stop-loss.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable tooling/settings note: the Fibonacci settings are described as deselecting everything and enabling only the wanted levels; the educator has 71% and 75% enabled and states he really only uses the 71%.
required_claims.transcript_quote: You just deselect everything and enable the levels you want. So I have the 71% and the 75%. Really only use the 71%.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (education): drawdown is defined as the time price spends in the area close to the stop loss.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Anytime that price is spending in this dark gray area close to my stop loss, that's considered draw down.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (education): the educator states drawdown and losing trades still occur even when all confluences line up.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Even if all the confluences line up, we sometimes still get draw down and losing trades.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (teaching intent): the second example is deliberately a non-textbook one.
required_claims.transcript_quote: What I like to do in these educational videos is provide an example that is textbook and then provide an example that is not so pretty.

required_claims.claim: description=Classification rule (education): a move is classified as a liquidity grab rather than a break of structure when it is a wick instead of a candle body closure.
required_claims.transcript_quote: The reason this is a liquidity grab instead of a break of structure is because it was a wick instead of candle body closure.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (education): a wick of that kind is described as indicating there was not enough momentum to break through and continue.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Whenever a wick is forming like that, that means there was not enough momentum to actually break through and continue.

required_claims.claim: description=Definition (education): relative equal highs are described as another form of liquidity.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, this is actually another form of liquidity called relative equal highs.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example): in the NZDUSD example the imbalance / fair value gap is identified on the chart.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now, we definitely have an imbalance here or fair value gap.

required_claims.claim: description=Context/rationale for the order type: the trade is set up in advance, which the educator ties to using a pending limit order.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now, because we're setting up a trade in advance, you would have to do a pending limit order, which means you're betting that price will get to this point at some point in time.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example observation, GBP AUD): the entry area was exceeded past the 71 and slightly past the 75, described by the educator as minimal drawdown.
required_claims.transcript_quote: You can see that it pushed past the 71, a little bit past the 75, but overall that is very minimal draw down in the grand scheme of things.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example observation, NZDUSD): price entered at the 71% and crossed the 75% with drawdown described as very minimal.
required_claims.transcript_quote: price entered at the 71% still crossed the 75% but the the draw down was very minimal.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (worked example observation, GBP AUD): the low made during the aggressive drop did not violate the low of the Fibonacci range.
required_claims.transcript_quote: You can see that this low here did not violate the low of the Fibonacci range.

required_claims.claim: description=Context (non-executable applicability claim): the educator names metals, indices, and reported cryptocurrency use.
required_claims.transcript_quote: It's also great for metals and indices and I also know a lot of people who use it in the cryptocurrency market.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable practice advice: applying the strategy on a demo account or on backtesting platforms is offered as acceptable.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Even if it's on a demo account or a platform like FX Replay or Tradezela back testing, that's fine, too.

required_claims.claim: description=Non-executable trading philosophy: the educator states his advocacy for mechanical trading strategies.
required_claims.transcript_quote: I'm a huge advocate for mechanical trading strategies.

required_claims.claim: action=Gauge premium and discount pricing on the trading range as the basis of higher time frame alignment. | rationale=Higher time frame alignment is the first checklist item and the educator defines its premise as premium and discount.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, the premise of higher time frame alignment is premium and discount. Whenever we have a trading range, we want to gauge premium and discount pricing.

required_claims.claim: action=When price is above 50% of the trading range (premium), look only for selling opportunities. | rationale=This is the stated directional filter produced by the premium reading.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, anything above 50% of the trading range is considered premium and we should only be looking for selling opportunities.

required_claims.claim: action=When price is below 50% of the trading range (discount), look only for buying opportunities. | rationale=This is the stated directional filter produced by the discount reading.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now, anything below the 50% is considered discount pricing and we would only want to be looking for buying opportunities.

required_claims.claim: action=Identify a liquidity sweep before getting involved in a trade. | rationale=Liquidity sweep is the second checklist item and the educator frames its identification as coming before trade involvement.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So there's two main reasons why a liquidity sweep is so important to identify before you get involved in a trade.

required_claims.claim: action=Look for the resting liquidity at major highs and major lows. | rationale=The educator names these as the most common areas where resting liquidity is found.
required_claims.transcript_quote: The most common area to find resting liquidity is major highs and major lows.

required_claims.claim: action=Treat liquidity already purged to the upside as favoring selling opportunities. | rationale=This is the directional inference the educator draws from the buyside sweep in the GBP AUD example.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now this tells us that there's a high likelihood of selling opportunities being favored now because the liquidity was already purged to the upside.

required_claims.claim: action=Treat a break of structure occurring in the market as the signal of a potential trade. | rationale=The educator states the break of structure is what signals a potential trade.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Whenever we have a break of structure occurring in the market that is signaling a potential trade.

required_claims.claim: action=Do not enter immediately when the break of structure occurs. | rationale=Immediate entry is explicitly rejected by the educator as contrary to the buy-low/sell-high premise.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So we don't just immediately enter when there's a break of structure because that would be selling low and we don't want to do that obviously.

required_claims.claim: action=After the break of structure, wait patiently for a retracement. | rationale=The educator states the required patience for a retracement following the break of structure.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So when a break of structure occurs, we need to patiently wait for a retracement.

required_claims.claim: action=Expect that retracement to be toward a fair value gap or imbalance. | rationale=The educator states this as the typical destination of the retracement, at 'typically' strength rather than as an absolute.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now, typically that retracement ends up being towards a fair value gap or an imbalance.

required_claims.claim: action=Draw the Fibonacci retracement tool by starting at the low, clicking, and dragging to the high, as narrated in the NZDUSD buy-side worked example. | rationale=This is the Fibonacci drawing procedure narrated in that worked example, which produces the retracement numbers used to frame the trade.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, all I do is break out the Fibonacci tool, start at the low, click, and drag to the high.

required_claims.claim: action=Place the entry at the 71%, as narrated in the GBP AUD sell-side worked example using the short position tool. | rationale=The 71% retracement is the fourth checklist item and this is where the educator places the entry in the sell-side worked example.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So using the short position tool on Trading View, I place my entry at the 71% right here.

required_claims.claim: action=Use a pending limit order for the entry. | rationale=The educator states the order type requirement explicitly for this strategy.
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, it's really important to note you have to use pending limit orders for this strategy.

required_claims.claim: description=The educator names an additional confluence, not on the checklist, in which the Fibonacci retracement number lines up with the imbalance or fair value gap. | name=Fibonacci retracement number aligned with the imbalance / fair value gap
required_claims.transcript_quote: And that is when the Fibonacci retracement number lines up with the imbalance or fair value gap.

required_claims.claim: description=The educator states that lining the entry up with the fair value gap makes it likely there will not be significant drawdown; this is stated at 'odds are' strength, not as a guarantee. | name=Reduced-drawdown expectation from entry aligned with the fair value gap
required_claims.transcript_quote: So if we can line up our entry with that fair value gap, odds are we're not going to have significant draw down.

required_claims.claim: description=The educator restates the confluence as an instruction to make the Fibonacci numbers line up with the fair value gap or imbalance. | name=Restated instruction to align Fibonacci numbers with the imbalance
required_claims.transcript_quote: Make your Fibonacci numbers line up with the fair value gap or imbalance.

required_claims.claim: description=The educator labels the combination of that confluence with the listed checklist items an A+ setup with a very high likelihood of success. | name=A+ setup label when the confluence is combined with the checklist items
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, if you can do that combined with the other things that I've listed here, that is what I like to call an A+ setup and you have a very high likelihood of success.

required_claims.claim: description=In the GBP AUD sell-side example the educator identifies the recent major lows as pretty untested relative equal lows. | name=Untested relative equal lows as the downside liquidity objective
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, those are pretty untested relative equal lows.

required_claims.claim: description=In the NZDUSD buy-side example the educator states sellside liquidity has already been purged while buyside liquidity has not, because of relative equal highs. | name=Sellside liquidity purged while buyside liquidity remains
required_claims.transcript_quote: So, we know that sellside liquidity has already been purged, but buyside liquidity was not purged because these are relative equal highs.

required_claims.claim: description=In the NZDUSD buy-side example the educator states that because relative equal highs were made, price is highly likely to push higher once more and take out that liquidity. | name=Relative equal highs implying a further push higher
required_claims.transcript_quote: But because we made these relative equal highs, that tells me price is highly likely to push higher once more, taking out all of this liquidity.

required_claims.claim: anchor=the high of the Fibonacci range (as placed in the GBP AUD sell-side worked example) | rationale=In the GBP AUD sell-side worked example the educator drags the stop-loss to the high of the Fibonacci range.
required_claims.transcript_quote: I simply drag the stop-loss to the high of the Fibonacci range right here.

required_claims.claim: type=take-profit dragged to the low of the Fibonacci range (GBP AUD sell-side worked example) | rationale=In the GBP AUD sell-side worked example the educator drags the take-profit to the low of the Fibonacci range.
required_claims.transcript_quote: And then I drag the takerit to the low of the Fibonacci range right here.

required_claims.claim: type=take-profit dragged to the high of the Fibonacci range (NZDUSD buy-side worked example) | rationale=In the NZDUSD buy-side worked example the educator drags the take-profit to the high of the Fibonacci range; this is the buy-side counterpart placement, narrated in the second example.
required_claims.transcript_quote: Same thing goes for my takerit. Click this little button at the top, drag it to the high of the Fibonacci range, and drop it.

required_claims.claim: rule=When the trade is based on a given high and low, the trade remains valid until one of those levels is violated.
required_claims.transcript_quote: That's a very important detail because if our trade was based on this high and this low, then technically the trade still remains valid until one of those levels are violated.

required_claims.claim: rule=While neither of those levels has been violated, the trade idea is still intact and the order is not to be deleted.
required_claims.transcript_quote: If neither of those levels have been violated, then the trade idea is still intact and there's logically no reason to delete the order.

required_claims.claim: rule=On the buy side the entry is placed at the 71% using the long position tool, after the Fibonacci tool is set up. | name=Buy-side entry placement (NZDUSD example)
required_claims.transcript_quote: So now that the fib tool is all set up, I can then click the long position tool on trading view and place my entry at the 71%.

required_claims.claim: rule=On the buy side the stop loss is clicked and dragged over to that wick, snapping to it with the magnet tool. | name=Buy-side stop placement (NZDUSD example)
required_claims.transcript_quote: Now using the magnet tool again, I can click the stop loss, drag it over to that wick, and it'll snap right to it.

required_claims.claim: rule=A break of structure that is not very clear and is described as internal is still counted as a break of structure. | name=Internal break of structure accepted (NZDUSD example)
required_claims.transcript_quote: The break of structure is not very clear here. This is more so an internal breakup structure, but it is a breaker structure nonetheless.
